narrative:
After carefully reviewing your application, the admissions process — which relies on a predictive assessment of bar exam readiness — determined that there is a 57% likelihood you would not pass the bar exam on your first attempt, which led to the rejection of your application. While this is not an overwhelming probability, it was sufficient to raise serious concerns about your preparedness for the rigors of law school and the bar exam that follows.

The single most influential factor working against your application was your LSAT score of 25. Among students who successfully passed the bar exam, the average LSAT score was approximately 37, meaning your score falls significantly below what is typically seen in students who go on to succeed. The LSAT is widely regarded as one of the strongest predictors of bar exam performance, and this gap was the primary driver of the model's concern about your application. That said, not everything in your profile pointed in a negative direction. Your third-year academic standing — the decile you occupied in your school based on Year 3 grades — actually worked in your favor, suggesting that you have demonstrated some capacity for sustained academic effort over time, and this partially offset the concerns raised by your LSAT score. Unfortunately, your first-year academic performance, where you ranked in the bottom decile of your school, reinforced the worries introduced by your LSAT, indicating that the early stages of your legal education were particularly challenging for you.

Beyond these three key factors, your profile includes other elements worth reflecting on. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.40 is notably lower than the 3.24 average among students who passed the bar, and you are enrolled part-time, a path taken by fewer than 7% of students who successfully passed — both of which suggest additional pressures on your academic performance. As a Hispanic male from an upper-middle income family, your background is well-represented among admitted students in terms of financial standing, which is a neutral factor in this assessment.

As a next step, you are strongly encouraged to retake the LSAT with dedicated preparation, as improving that score would have the most meaningful impact on a future application. Seeking academic support resources, building on the upward trajectory your third-year grades suggest, and considering whether full-time enrollment might be feasible could all strengthen your candidacy considerably.
